turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files describing perovskite solar cells as
complete devices — `substrate` (glass + transparent electrode), `etl`
(electron-transport layer stack), `htl` (hole-transport layer stack),
`backcontact` (metal / carbon back electrode), `deposition` (absorber
deposition procedure; `>>` separates steps). Every candidate below uses the
same MAPbI3 absorber in the same n-i-p (regular) architecture; they differ
only in the remaining columns. Each row is a device CONFIGURATION whose
efficiency is the median over at least 3 independently fabricated cells, so
it is a reproducible recipe rather than a single champion cell:
  - b3_pvk_stack_train.csv: 300 configurations with the measured power
    conversion efficiency (%).
  - b3_pvk_stack_pool.csv: 100 CANDIDATE configurations whose power
    conversion efficiency (%) was NOT measured, columns `candidate_id` and
    the same device columns.

Using the training data, select the 5 candidates with the HIGHEST power
conversion efficiency (%).

Reason from the device physics — band alignment and selectivity of the
transport layers, interface recombination, contact chemistry and the film
quality the process is likely to give — then end your answer with an
explicit ranked list of candidate_ids, best first, e.g. "Final: c901, c902,
c903, c904, c905".
turns.answer_text:
My predicted top five are **c064, c005, c068, c017, and c013**, in that order. I weighted close, high-performing training analogues most heavily, then considered whether the candidate’s changes should improve charge selectivity, suppress interfacial recombination, or improve contact quality. These are predictions—not measured efficiencies—and the last few positions are uncertain.

| Rank | Candidate | Training evidence and device-physics rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **c064** | **TiO2-c / SnO2-np / Spiro-MeOTAD / Au.** The closest ETL configuration in training reaches **20.85%**, although with Ag and an additional dip-coating step. Another TiO2-c/SnO2 configuration gives **17.47%** using spin-coating. The compact TiO2 layer can block holes and prevent direct absorber–electrode contact, while the SnO2 overlayer provides an electron-selective absorber interface. Together with Spiro-MeOTAD/Au, this is the strongest combination of nearby measured performance and plausible selective contacts. I would not transfer the 20.85% value directly because the deposition procedure differs. |
| **2** | **c005** | **TiO2-c / PCBM-60 / PCDTBT8 / MoO3 / Au.** A particularly close training analogue—FTO instead of ITO and PCDTBT1 instead of PCDTBT8—achieves **19.35%**. PCBM can improve electron extraction and reduce recombination at the oxide/perovskite interface; MoO3 can improve the hole-contact interface with Au. The major uncertainty is the different PCDTBT derivative: its energy levels, mobility, and film coverage cannot be assumed identical. Nevertheless, this candidate closely resembles one of the best measured complete stacks. |
| **3** | **c068** | **SnO2-np / TiO2-np / PTAA / Au–MoO3.** The training device with SnO2-np/PTAA/Ag reaches **18.19%**, while SnO2/TiO2 bilayers with Spiro-MeOTAD reach **16.54%**. This supports a relatively high ranking for an oxide-bilayer/PTAA device. PTAA provides hole selectivity and electron blocking; a well-formed oxide bilayer can improve coverage and suppress leakage. Its benefit depends on avoiding an extraction barrier or additional traps at the oxide–oxide interface. |
| **4** | **c017** | **Fullerene-based ETL / doped TaTm HTL / Ag, co-evaporated.** This is nearly the same configuration as the **17.9%** training device with Au. The fullerene contact provides electron selectivity, while F6-TCNNQ-doped TaTm supports conductive hole extraction. Co-evaporation also offers controlled absorber thickness and coverage. The Au-to-Ag substitution introduces uncertainty through work-function differences and possible iodide–silver chemistry, but the unusually close training match makes this a strong choice. |
| **5** | **c013** | **TiO2-c / P(VDF-TrFE)–Spiro-MeOTAD / MoO3–Ag.** Training contains high-performing TiO2-based devices with modified hole-side interfaces, including **18.965%** for IEICO-4F/Spiro-MeOTAD/MoO3–Ag. A sufficiently thin P(VDF-TrFE) interlayer could reduce interfacial recombination and alter local electrostatics while retaining extraction through Spiro-MeOTAD. This is the most speculative selection: an overly thick insulating polymer layer would instead reduce fill factor. |

I favor these over HTL-free carbon configurations, bare ZnO interfaces, and poorly selective contacts, which generally have weaker training support or greater recombination/contact-chemistry risks.

Final: c064, c005, c068, c017, c013
